claim: Burn injuries are a leading cause of unintentional injury.
source: Burn injuries are a major health issue globally, ranking among the leading causes of unintentional injury, and non-surgical treatment options are mostly limited to supportive clinical care (Peck, 2011; Boldeanu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peck, 2011 and Boldeanu et al., 2020

claim: Major burn trauma results in dysfunctional immune responses.
source: Major burn trauma results in dysfunctional immune responses and is associated with an increased risk of infections leading to poor survival outcomes (Moins-Teisserenc et al., 2021; Bergquist et al., 2019; Jeschke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moins-Teisserenc et al., 2021; Bergquist et al., 2019; Jeschke et al., 2014

claim: Major burn trauma is associated with an increased risk of infections leading to poor survival outcomes.
source: Major burn trauma results in dysfunctional immune responses and is associated with an increased risk of infections leading to poor survival outcomes (Moins-Teisserenc et al., 2021; Bergquist et al., 2019; Jeschke et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moins-Teisserenc et al., 2021; Bergquist et al., 2019; Jeschke et al., 2014

claim: Serum levels of IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, and IFN-γ are significantly higher in burn trauma patients compared to non-burn.
source: Serum levels of interleukin (IL)–6, IL-10, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, and interferon (IFN)-γ are significantly higher in burn trauma patients compared to non-burn (Mace et al., 2012; Finnerty et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mace et al., 2012; Finnerty et al., 2007

claim: Higher serum concentrations of IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, GM-CSF, IL-12p70, IFN-γ, and TNF-α are associated with sepsis and death in children with severe burns.
source: Similarly, higher serum concentrations of IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, GM-CSF, IL-12p70, IFN-γ, and TNF-α, are associated with sepsis and death in children with severe burns (Finnerty et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finnerty et al., 2007

claim: There is a paucity of studies examining the local immune response of injured burn tissue in humans.
source: Despite the many studies in this area that examine immune responses in blood to understand the systemic effects of burn injury, there is a paucity of studies examining the local immune response of injured burn tissue in humans.
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature

claim: Most reports characterizing T cells in the skin after a burn injury have been in mice.
source: Most reports characterizing T cells in the skin after a burn injury have been in mice (Daniel et al., 2007; Rani et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2011; Rani and Schwacha, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Daniel et al., 2007; Rani et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2011; Rani and Schwacha, 2017

claim: αβ T cells and γδ T cells show increased production of cytokines TNF-α, IL-10, and IFN-γ in the days following burn injury in mice.
source: In particular, αβ T cells and gamma-delta (γδ) T cells show increased production of cytokines TNF-α, IL-10, and IFN-γ in the days following burn injury (Rani et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rani et al., 2014

claim: A significant number of αβ T cells and γδ T cells infiltrate the burn site in mice.
source: A significant number of αβ T cells and γδ T cells infiltrate the burn site, causing a total decrease in CD69+ cells, a marker of tissue residency in T cells (Rani et al., 2015; Schenkel and Masopust, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rani et al., 2015; Schenkel and Masopust, 2014

claim: Infiltration of αβ T cells and γδ T cells to the burn site causes a total decrease in CD69+ cells in mice.
source: A significant number of αβ T cells and γδ T cells infiltrate the burn site, causing a total decrease in CD69+ cells, a marker of tissue residency in T cells (Rani et al., 2015; Schenkel and Masopust, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rani et al., 2015; Schenkel and Masopust, 2014

claim: CD69 is a marker of tissue residency in T cells.

evidence: Supported by citations to Rani et al., 2015; Schenkel and Masopust, 2014

claim: Knockout of γδ T cells results in significantly higher TNF-α levels in the skin of mice following burn injury.
source: Knockout of γδ T cells results in significantly higher TNF-α levels in the skin of mice following burn injury, suggesting a major role of γδ T cells in negating a pro-inflammatory environment (Daniel et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daniel et al., 2007

claim: γδ T cells play a major role in negating a pro-inflammatory environment in mouse burn injury.

evidence: Supported by citation to Daniel et al., 2007 and inference from knockout data

claim: γδ T cells account for >50% of total T cells in mouse skin.

evidence: Supported by citations to Ebert et al., 2006; Mestas and Hughes, 2004

claim: γδ T cells account for 2–5% of total T cells in human skin.

claim: The impact of acute inflammatory insults such as burns on TRM and TCM populations remains unknown.
